### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Of all things the measure is man.”

Ancient Greek

“πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἐστὶν ἄνθρωπος.”

“Of all things the measure is man.” Survives as a fragment (DK 80B1) quoted by Plato in the Theaetetus; we do not have Protagoras' own book.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Man is the measure of all things.”
-   “Of all things the measure is man.”

### Attribution notes

Protagoras DK 80B1, preserved through Plato's Theaetetus 152a. Plato immediately presses the fragment into a relativist reading about perception; whether Protagoras meant that, or something narrower about human standards of judgment, is exactly the dispute the dialogue stages. Quoting the English alone as a finished doctrine skips that problem.

#### About Protagoras

Protagoras (c. 490–c.

### Interpretation

Protagoras's measure doctrine is usually read as relativism, and Plato's Theaetetus — our source — pushes it that way. The Greek is ambiguous: "of all things" may mean things are as they appear to each person, or that a human being is the standard for judging them. Either reading made the claim famous and contested, since it appears to remove any court of appeal above individual appearance.

#### Why it matters

The difficulty it raises is still live: if disagreement is settled by whose appearance counts, there is no disagreement to settle — which suggests the doctrine cannot be stated coherently.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Of all things the measure is man.”?

“Of all things the measure is man.” comes from DK, 80B1 (via Plato, Theaetetus), attributed to Protagoras.

#### What does Protagoras mean by knowledge?

Epistemology asks whether knowledge is justified true belief, reliable tracking of the world, or something else; it also asks how perception, testimony, memory, and reason contribute. This passage enters that discussion through knowledge, humanity.

#### Is the wording of this Protagoras quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Of all things the measure is man.” Forms in circulation that differ: Man is the measure of all things. / Of all things the measure is man. The Ancient Greek reads “πάντων χρημάτων μέτρον ἐστὶν ἄνθρωπος.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Protagoras DK 80B1, preserved through Plato's Theaetetus 152a. Plato immediately presses the fragment into a relativist reading about perception; whether Protagoras meant that, or something narrower about human standards of judgment, is exactly the dispute the dialogue stages. Quoting the English alone as a finished doctrine skips that problem.
